 Medicare Advantage Plans Require Careful Review Before Enrollment

 A Medicare Advantage PPO card rests on top of a Medicare card in Portland, Ore., on June 10, 2024. Jenny Kane, AP file. 
 Smallest Font 
 Largest Font 
 Older Americans considering Medicare Advantage coverage face important decisions about healthcare costs, provider access and insurance restrictions. Information published November 6-7, 2026, highlights how these plans compare with traditional Medicare, particularly for seniors in rural communities who may need specialized medical services outside their local areas. Medicare Advantage plans, offered by private insurance companies, can provide lower monthly premiums and additional benefits, including dental coverage, vision care, fitness programs and meal delivery.
 However, the availability and extent of these benefits vary by plan, according to KFF's Medicare guidance published November 6, 2026. Although these plans can include supplemental benefits unavailable through traditional Medicare, they must still cover the same services covered by traditional Medicare. Some additional benefits, including dental coverage, may require an extra monthly premium, KFF explained.

 Healthcare access presents another consideration for residents of rural areas. A November 6 letter published by The Daily Bulldog highlighted concerns affecting seniors in Franklin County, Maine, where specialized treatment may require travel to Lewiston, Augusta, Portland or Boston.
 Also Read 
 US Prescription Drug Policies Trigger Global Price Concerns 
 Original Medicare generally allows beneficiaries to visit doctors and hospitals nationwide that accept Medicare. Medicare Advantage plans typically use provider networks, meaning treatment outside those networks can involve higher expenses, additional approval requirements or limited coverage, except for certain services such as emergency care. Financial considerations also extend beyond monthly premiums.
 Medicare Advantage beneficiaries may face copayments and coinsurance for hospital stays, specialist appointments, diagnostic procedures and rehabilitation. Although these plans establish annual out-of-pocket limits for covered Medicare Part A and Part B services, those limits can still reach thousands of dollars.
 By comparison, Original Medicare combined with a Medicare Supplement Insurance policy, commonly known as Medigap, generally involves higher monthly premiums but can offer broader provider access and more predictable healthcare expenses. Prior authorization is another important distinction. Medicare Advantage insurers frequently require approval before beneficiaries receive certain services, including rehabilitation, skilled nursing care and some diagnostic procedures.
 Also Read 
 Florida Nurse Describes Being Trapped by Patient Relative 
 The Daily Bulldog letter also referenced federal oversight reports documenting cases in which Medicare Advantage plans denied requests for services that would have satisfied Medicare coverage requirements. Such restrictions can create additional difficulties for rural patients coordinating specialist appointments and transportation. Insurance coverage can also change annually, even when beneficiaries remain with the same insurer.
 Provider networks, prescription drug formularies, deductibles, copayments and prior authorization requirements may be revised, potentially affecting access to established doctors and medications. Switching coverage later presents additional challenges. Beneficiaries generally can return to Original Medicare during applicable enrollment periods, but obtaining a Medigap policy may involve separate eligibility requirements.
 Outside certain guaranteed-issue protections, Medigap insurers may consider an applicant's medical history when deciding whether to issue coverage. Maine provides additional consumer protections, but eligibility requirements and time limits apply, according to The Daily Bulldog's November 6 report.
 Also Read 
 Insurers Cut Medicare Advantage Plans for 1 Million Seniors in 2027 
 For residents of western Maine, SeniorsPlus offers nonprofit assistance with Medicare decisions and other programs affecting older adults and people with disabilities. The organization provides an alternative source of guidance to insurance agents and brokers, whose compensation may include commissions from insurance companies when customers enroll in particular plans. The Yakima Herald also addressed Medicare Advantage enrollment in a November 7 editorial, emphasizing the importance of examining policy details before signing up. Differences in coverage, costs and provider access remain important considerations when comparing available Medicare options.
